778.title: Vana: exile
778.hook: Krishna comes to the forest, Draupadi tells him everything, and he explains why he wasn't there
778.howItsDone: Devotees revere Krishna as God, and storytellers dwell on this forest meeting, where Draupadi pours out her grief and Krishna promises that the wrongs done to her will be answered.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Vana, the forest, the sun gave Yudhishthira a vessel, and Draupadi served everyone before herself. Your line was Vana: exile. Did you pour for someone else first? Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

Chariots on a forest road. Word has reached Krishna's people that the Pandavas are in exile, and Krishna comes to find them, with kinsmen beside him. The cousins embrace. And then Draupadi speaks. She doesn't make small talk. She tells him everything: the hall, being dragged in by her hair, the laughter, the husbands who sat silent. She weeps as she speaks. And under all of it is one question she doesn't quite need to say out loud. Where were you? Today, Krishna in the forest, and his answer.
screen: `KRISHNA COMES TO THE FOREST.` → `DRAUPADI TELLS EVERYTHING.` → `WHERE WERE YOU?`

segments.voice: Notice first what Draupadi does with her grief. She doesn't tidy it. She names each wrong, in order, to the one person she trusts to hear it whole. In the epic's telling, she even says that she has no husband, no son, no friend, no brother, and not even Krishna, because none of them protected her. That is a hard thing to say to someone's face. And Krishna doesn't argue with it. He makes her a promise instead: the women of those who wronged her will one day weep as she is weeping now. Then, turning to Yudhishthira, he answers the question underneath. I wasn't there, he says. If I had been in Dvaraka, I would have come to that game uninvited and stopped it. But he was away, fighting a king named Shalva, who had attacked his city in a flying citadel. By the time he came home and heard the news, the dice had already fallen. It's a striking moment. Krishna, whom devotees worship as God, here gives an account of his absence. He doesn't say the suffering was meant to happen. He doesn't tell Draupadi to be calm. He says, in effect, I was fighting somewhere else, and had I been home, I would have stopped it. So the forest becomes a place for this kind of conversation too. Away from the palace, away from the hall, Draupadi says exactly what she thinks, even to Krishna, and Krishna stays to hear all of it before he answers.
screen: `DRAUPADI NAMES EACH WRONG.` · `KRISHNA MAKES A PROMISE.` · `I WAS FIGHTING SHALVA.` · then, large: `GRIEF SAID OUT LOUD, AND HEARD.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind someone who once told you something hard: a hurt, a complaint, maybe even one that was about you. Remember how it felt to hear it. Now, with each breath out, let yourself simply listen, the way Krishna listens before he answers. No fixing, no defending. Breathe in, and make room. Breathe out, and stay. If you pray, you can bring that person into your prayer. If not, just hold them kindly in mind. The bell holds the time.
Vana. The forest of exile, where Draupadi tells Krishna everything, and Krishna says where he was.
Your line: Vana: exile. Today, when someone tells you something hard, let them finish before you answer. Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

779.title: Vana: exile
779.hook: in the forest, Draupadi argues for anger and Yudhishthira argues for forgiveness, and the epic lets them both speak
779.howItsDone: Teachers and commentators return to this forest debate between Draupadi and Yudhishthira when discussing anger, forgiveness and right action, and Prahlada's answer to Bali is retold on its own as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday Krishna came to the Vana, the forest, and Draupadi told him everything. Your line was Vana: exile. Did you let someone finish before you answered? Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

An evening in the forest, and a married couple is having a real argument. Draupadi looks at her husband in his bark clothes, sleeping on the ground, and she can't stand it. You were a king, she says. Your brothers are suffering. How is your anger not blazing? Yudhishthira doesn't storm out. He answers her, at length. And she answers back. The epic doesn't cut this scene short or tell us who won. It gives both of them the floor. Today, the great forest argument: anger or forgiveness?
screen: `A COUPLE ARGUES IN THE FOREST.` → `WHY IS YOUR ANGER NOT BLAZING?` → `BOTH OF THEM GET THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Draupadi doesn't argue from feeling alone. She brings a story. Long ago, she says, the demon king Bali asked his grandfather Prahlada, the same Prahlada whose verdict Vidura told in the hall, a question: which is better, forgiveness or might? And Prahlada answered: neither one, always. Someone who forgives everything is treated with contempt, even by his own servants. Someone who never forgives makes enemies of everyone. There's a time for each, and wisdom is knowing which time it is. Now, says Draupadi, is the time for might. Yudhishthira answers with a different picture. Anger, he says, is the root of destruction. An angry person can't tell what should be said from what shouldn't, and will harm even those who deserve no harm. Forgiveness, in his telling, is what holds the world together; if there were no one who forgave, there would be no peace among people at all. He calls forgiveness the strength of the strong. So who is right? This is what makes the scene worth sitting with. Draupadi isn't the hothead and Yudhishthira isn't the saint. Both of them quote the wisdom of their tradition. Both of them are suffering. Draupadi's point is about timing: forgiveness offered always can become weakness. Yudhishthira's point is about the self: anger acted on can burn the one who carries it. And the forest is where they can say all this. There's no court here, no audience of kings. Just two people who lost the same things, disagreeing honestly about what to do next.
screen: `PRAHLADA: A TIME FOR EACH.` · `DRAUPADI: NOW IS THE TIME FOR MIGHT.` · `YUDHISHTHIRA: ANGER DESTROYS.` · then, large: `BOTH QUOTE THEIR TRADITION.`

segments.voice: Let yourself settle, and feel your feet or your seat. Bring to mind one thing that still makes you angry. Not the biggest; a medium one will do. Breathe in, and let Draupadi's question rise: is this a time for strength? Breathe out, and let Yudhishthira's rise: what would this anger do to me if I carried it? You don't need to settle the argument. Just let both voices speak while you breathe. If you pray, you can bring that situation into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Vana. The forest of exile, where Draupadi argues for might and Yudhishthira for forgiveness, and both are heard.
Your line: Vana: exile. Today, before you act on anger, ask the question Prahlada answered: is this a time for strength, or a time to let go? Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

780.title: Vana: exile
780.hook: Bhima wants to fight now, and Yudhishthira holds to the word he gave in the hall
780.howItsDone: Yudhishthira's insistence on keeping his word in exile is held up in Hindu storytelling as a picture of satya, truthfulness, and is discussed alongside Bhima's very different temperament.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Vana, Draupadi argued for might and Yudhishthira for forgiveness. Your line was Vana: exile. When anger came, did you ask whether it was a time for strength? Day seven hundred eighty.

Bhima has been listening, and he's done waiting. He's built for action, strong and impatient. He's watched his brothers live on roots and his wife sleep on the ground, and he can't see the point of it. Our enemies cheated, he says. Why are we keeping faith with cheats? Let's go back and take what's ours. It's a fair question, and he asks it loudly. Today, the brother who wants to fight, and the brother who gave his word.
screen: `BHIMA IS DONE WAITING.` → `WHY KEEP FAITH WITH CHEATS?` → `THE BROTHER WHO GAVE HIS WORD.`

segments.voice: Bhima's case is strong, and the epic lets him make it in full. The game was a trap. Time is passing. Every day in the forest is a day their enemies grow stronger. And a warrior who sits still, he says, is failing at his own duty. Yudhishthira hears him out, and then he answers with one thing. I gave my word. In the hall, in front of everyone, he agreed to the terms of the last throw: the years in the forest, then a year in hiding. Breaking that promise now, he says, would be worse to him than losing the kingdom. He would rather keep his word than win by breaking it. The old word for what he's holding on to is satya: truth, and also truthfulness, being someone whose word holds. Then Yudhishthira adds something more practical, and more honest. Even if they wanted to fight now, he says, look who stands on the other side: Bhishma, Drona, Karna, great warriors all. We aren't ready. So the forest isn't only a punishment to be endured. It's time. Time to keep a promise, and time to prepare. Bhima's frustration isn't wrong, and the epic doesn't mock it. But Yudhishthira's refusal isn't weakness either. It's a man deciding that who he is matters more than how fast he gets his kingdom back. A stubborn sense of what he owes also walked him back to the dice board when the old king summoned him. Here in the forest, it keeps four brothers and a wife waiting with him under the trees.
screen: `BHIMA: WHY WAIT?` · `YUDHISHTHIRA: I GAVE MY WORD.` · `SATYA: A WORD THAT HOLDS.` · then, large: `THE FOREST IS ALSO TIME.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle, and the breath slow down. Bring to mind a promise you're keeping that has turned out to be harder than you expected. A commitment, a job, a way you said you'd treat someone. Let the Bhima in you speak first: why not just drop it? Breathe with that. Then let the Yudhishthira in you speak: who would I be if I did? Breathe with that too. You don't have to decide anything now. If you pray, you can hold that promise in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Vana. The forest of exile, where Bhima wants to fight now and Yudhishthira keeps the word he gave in the hall.
Your line: Vana: exile. Today, keep one small word you gave, exactly as you gave it, even if no one would notice if you didn't. Day seven hundred eighty.

781.title: Vana: exile
781.hook: Vyasa walks into the forest camp with a plan: the waiting can become preparation, and Arjuna must go alone
781.howItsDone: Retellings of the Mahabharata mark Vyasa's visit as the turn in the forest years, when Arjuna leaves to seek divine weapons; tradition names Vyasa as the epic's composer as well as a character in it.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Vana, Bhima wanted to fight and Yudhishthira kept his word. Your line was Vana: exile. Did you keep one small word exactly as you gave it? Day seven hundred eighty-one.

The argument has gone as far as it can go. Bhima wants them stronger, and soon. Yudhishthira won't break his word, and he knows how formidable the warriors on the other side are. The brothers are stuck between impatience and patience. And into that stuck place walks an old sage. It's Vyasa, the grandfather of both the Pandavas and the Kauravas, and he has come with a way out. Today, the visitor who turns waiting into a plan.
screen: `STUCK BETWEEN IMPATIENCE AND PATIENCE.` → `VYASA WALKS IN.` → `WAITING BECOMES A PLAN.`

segments.voice: Vyasa takes Yudhishthira aside. I know what's in your heart, he says, the fear of Bhishma and Drona and Karna. So here's what to do. He gives Yudhishthira a sacred knowledge to teach to Arjuna, a kind of inner discipline that will let him reach the gods. And he says: Arjuna must go. He must seek out the gods themselves, Indra and Rudra and the guardians of the world, and win their weapons through ascetic effort. That is how the Pandavas will be ready when the time of exile ends. Now the argument looks different. Bhima wanted action, and here it is. Yudhishthira wanted to keep his word, and he does. Nobody breaks the terms; nobody leaves the forest early. But the waiting stops being empty. It becomes a time to grow. And then notice the cost. Arjuna has to go alone. The brothers who have shared everything, even exile, will be apart. Yudhishthira teaches him what Vyasa taught, and Arjuna prepares to leave, armed, toward the mountains of the north. In the epic, Draupadi speaks a blessing over him as he goes, wishing him success and asking that the gods protect him on the road. Vana, the forest, has carried the Pandavas through a lot: the sun's vessel, Krishna's visit, the long arguments. Now it becomes something else, a base camp. One brother walks out of it, and tomorrow we follow him up the mountain.
screen: `VYASA TAKES YUDHISHTHIRA ASIDE.` · `A KNOWLEDGE FOR ARJUNA.` · `SEEK THE WEAPONS OF THE GODS.` · then, large: `THE WAITING BECOMES GROWING.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and let the breath become slow and easy. Bring to mind some waiting in your own life: a season you can't hurry, an answer that hasn't come. Breathe in, and feel how it sits in you. Breathe out, and ask, gently, what this waiting could be for. Is there one small thing it could prepare you for? Don't force an answer; just let the question breathe with you. If you pray, you can bring that waiting into your prayer. If not, rest in the question. The bell holds the time.
Vana. The forest of exile, which becomes a base camp the day Vyasa sends Arjuna to seek the weapons of the gods.
Your line: Vana: exile. Today, take one stretch of waiting, a line, a commute, a slow afternoon, and use it to prepare for something. Day seven hundred eighty-one.

782.title: Arjuna's austerities
782.hook: on the mountain, a thin old ascetic tells Arjuna to throw away his bow, and Arjuna won't
782.howItsDone: Retellings of the Mahabharata follow Arjuna to the mountain, where Indra tests him in disguise before sending him to seek Shiva; the episode is part of the long tradition of tapas, ascetic effort, in Hindu stories.

segments.voice: Yesterday Vyasa came to the forest, and your line was Vana: exile. The waiting became a plan, and Arjuna set out alone. Did you use a stretch of waiting to prepare? Day seven hundred eighty-two.

Stop. The word rings out across a mountain slope in the north, and Arjuna stops. He has walked a long way, bow in hand, quiver on his back, toward a peak the epic calls Indrakila. Under a tree sits an ascetic, thin, matted hair, glowing with the strength of long discipline. And the ascetic looks at the armed young man and asks, more or less: what are you doing with those? This is a place of peace. Today the first test of Arjuna's austerities, and it doesn't look like a test at all.
screen: `STOP.` → `AN ASCETIC UNDER A TREE.` → `WHAT ARE YOU DOING WITH THOSE?`

segments.voice: The ascetic goes on. Here, he says, live peaceful seekers who have left anger behind. There's no need for weapons in this place. Throw away your bow. You've already reached a high state. It's a tempting offer, and he makes it again and again. But Arjuna won't put the bow down. He tells the ascetic he won't leave his brothers waiting in the forest and go off to some peaceful world without the weapons he came for. Then the ascetic shows who he really is. He's Indra, king of the gods, and Arjuna's own father in the story. He's pleased, and he offers his son a boon: ask for anything. Arjuna asks for weapons. And Indra answers: first, you must see Shiva, the three-eyed god who holds the trident. When you've seen him, I'll give you my own weapons. So the first lesson of Arjuna's austerities is a surprising one. The test isn't whether he can give everything up. It's whether he knows what he came for. Indra's offer of peace sounds holy, and in another life it might be his path. But Arjuna has a purpose, a family in the forest and a promise to keep, and he holds onto it even when a radiant ascetic tells him to let it go. Austerity, in this story, doesn't start with fasting. It starts with being clear about why you're there.
screen: `THROW AWAY YOUR BOW.` · `ARJUNA HOLDS ON.` · `IT WAS INDRA ALL ALONG.` · then, large: `FIRST, YOU MUST SEE SHIVA.`

segments.voice: Let yourself settle, and feel the weight of your body resting. Bring to mind something you're working toward right now, small or large. A task, a change, a person you're trying to show up for. Breathe in, and ask: why am I doing this? Breathe out, and let the answer be simple. If other voices come, telling you to drop it, let them pass like weather on a mountain. Come back to the why. If you pray, you can hold that purpose in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna's austerities. They begin on a mountain, where an ascetic tells him to throw away his bow, and Arjuna remembers why he came.
Your line: Arjuna's austerities. Today, before you start something, say to yourself in a few words why you're doing it. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

783.title: Arjuna's austerities
783.hook: the warrior becomes an ascetic, eating less and less, until the sages of the mountain go to Shiva about him
783.howItsDone: Tapas, disciplined austerity such as fasting, stillness and self-restraint, runs through Hindu stories and practice; Arjuna on the mountain is one of the epic's pictures of a seeker whose tapas draws a god's response.

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna's austerities began with a test: Indra, in disguise, told him to throw away his bow, and he wouldn't. Did you name your why before you started something? Day seven hundred eighty-three.

A warrior in grass clothes. That's what the sages on the mountain see when they look at the newcomer. Arjuna, prince and archer, has traded his royal dress for rags of grass and a deerskin, and taken up a staff. He's come to the foot of the Himalayas to do one thing: to draw the attention of Shiva. And the way he sets about it is tapas, the slow, burning work of austerity. Today, what Arjuna's austerities actually looked like, and what they did to the mountain.
screen: `A WARRIOR IN GRASS CLOTHES.` → `TO DRAW SHIVA'S ATTENTION.` → `THE BURNING WORK OF TAPAS.`

segments.voice: The epic describes it step by step. At first Arjuna eats fruit, but only every few nights. Then less often. Then less. Month by month he narrows his life, until at last he lives on air alone, standing on the tips of his toes with his arms raised, motionless. His hair, the text says, grows matted and bright. Now here's the strange part. His austerity isn't quiet. It gives off heat. In this story, tapas burns, and the burning is real. The sages who live on the mountain begin to feel it. Smoke, in the epic's telling, seems to rise from the earth around him. They grow worried. So they go to Shiva and say, more or less: who is this man, and what is he doing? His austerity is troubling us all. Shiva's answer is calm. Don't worry, he says. I know what's in Arjuna's heart. I know what he wants. Go back, and be at peace. So while Arjuna stands on his toes with his arms in the air, the god he came to find already knows what he's after. Arjuna hasn't said a word to Shiva. His discipline has spoken for him, loudly enough that the neighbors went to complain. On this mountain, at least, practice isn't private.
screen: `LESS FOOD, THEN ONLY AIR.` · `TAPAS GIVES OFF HEAT.` · `THE SAGES GO TO SHIVA.` · then, large: `SHIVA ALREADY KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Sit or stand, and let the body be still in whatever way is comfortable. You don't need to stand on your toes. Just notice the warmth of your own body: in the hands, the chest, the face. Breathe in, and feel that warmth. Breathe out, and let it settle. Bring to mind one small discipline you keep, or would like to keep. As you breathe, let it feel less like a burden and more like a little heat you carry. If you pray, you can offer that discipline in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna's austerities. Less food, then only air, a heat the sages felt, and a god who already knew what he wanted.
Your line: Arjuna's austerities. Today, keep one small discipline without announcing it, and trust that it's doing its work anyway. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

784.title: Arjuna's austerities
784.hook: a boar charges, two arrows strike it at once, and a mountain hunter says it was his
784.howItsDone: The meeting of Arjuna and Shiva as a hunter is retold in Hindu storytelling, poetry and temple art, and Shiva in the guise of a Kirata is honored as a form of the god.

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna's austerities burned so hot the sages went to Shiva, and Shiva said: I know what he wants. Did you keep a small discipline quietly? Day seven hundred eighty-four.

Crashing through the trees, a boar. It's huge, and it's coming straight at Arjuna. The story tells us it's no ordinary animal: a demon named Muka has taken this shape to kill the man at prayer. Thin from fasting, Arjuna still moves fast. He grabs his bow, nocks an arrow and draws. And at that very moment, someone else is drawing too. A hunter has stepped out of the forest, a Kirata, one of the mountain people, with a woman at his side and a crowd behind him. Two archers. One boar. Today, the hunter.
screen: `A BOAR CRASHES THROUGH THE TREES.` → `ARJUNA DRAWS HIS BOW.` → `SO DOES A HUNTER.`

segments.voice: The listener already knows something Arjuna doesn't. The hunter is Shiva. He's come down the mountain in disguise, and the woman beside him is his consort Uma, also disguised. Shiva told the sages, I know what he wants. Now he's come to see what Arjuna is made of. Stop, the hunter calls. I aimed at that boar first. Arjuna ignores him and shoots. So does the hunter. Both arrows strike at the same instant, and the boar falls dead, in its own demon shape again. And Arjuna is furious. Who are you, he demands, roaming this empty forest with women around you? Why did you shoot the game I had already marked? That breaks the rules of the hunt. I'll take your life for it. The hunter isn't impressed. This forest is our home, he says, more or less. I claimed that boar first. And if you think you're strong, shoot. This is the turn the whole week has been walking toward. In the forest, the Pandavas argued about anger and patience, about might and keeping their word. On the mountain, Arjuna held onto his purpose, and burned with tapas until the sages complained. And now, after all that discipline, the first person he meets makes him angry in seconds. The text doesn't hide it. Arjuna's austerities have made him strong. They haven't yet made him humble. And he's about to pick a fight with the very god he came to find.
screen: `THE HUNTER IS SHIVA IN DISGUISE.` · `TWO ARROWS, ONE BOAR.` · `ARJUNA: YOU BROKE THE RULES.` · then, large: `STRONG, BUT NOT YET HUMBLE.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle, and the breath slow. Think back over this week: the forest, the arguments, the waiting, the mountain. Now bring to mind a moment, maybe recent, when someone stepped into your way and you flared up. Breathe in, and see that person again. Breathe out, and wonder, just for a moment: what if they weren't who I thought they were? You don't have to excuse anything. Just leave that question open. If you pray, you can bring that moment into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna's austerities. They've made him strong enough to face a demon boar, and quick enough to pick a fight with a hunter who is Shiva.
Your line: Arjuna's austerities. Today, when someone gets in your way, give them one breath before you decide who they are. Day seven hundred eighty-four.
